name: Research Methods in Social Science
description: A core course introducing students to the philosophical foundations and practical tools of social science research — from developing research questions and reviewing literature to designing studies, collecting data, and communicating findings ethically and rigorously.

modules.title: Introduction to Social Science Research
modules.objectives: Define social science research and distinguish it from everyday inquiry; identify the major social science disciplines and their distinctive research questions; explain the relationship between theory and empirical research.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §1.2 — Science, Social Science, and Sociology
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Introduction to Social Science Research; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Introduction to Social Science Research evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Write a 350-word essay answering: What makes social science 'scientific'? Describe two ways that social science research differs from natural science research (e.g., the role of the researcher, studying humans who react to being observed), and two ways they are similar. Give one concrete example of a social science research question and explain what kind of evidence could answer it. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: the final product, visible work or evidence, and a short explanation connecting each conclusion to Introduction to Social Science Research. Evaluation: 100% total — Introduction to Social Science Research concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); quality of the concrete research-question example and comparison argument (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Philosophical Foundations of Research
modules.objectives: Distinguish between positivist, interpretivist, and critical research paradigms; explain the concepts of ontology and epistemology as they apply to social research; describe how philosophical assumptions shape research design choices.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §2.2 — Paradigms, Theories, and Research Approaches
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Philosophical Foundations of Research; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Philosophical Foundations of Research evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Classify each fictional claim by paradigm and justify the fit: A “weekly screen time can be measured objectively and modeled as a predictor of sleep”; B “students construct different meanings of online belonging through lived experience”; C “platform rules reproduce power differences and should be examined with affected groups.” For each, state a likely ontology, epistemology, research question, and suitable method. Then explain one limitation of treating any paradigm as automatically superior. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: a three-row comparison table using all supplied claims, ontology, epistemology, question, method, and three evidence-based justifications. Evaluation: 100% total — Research Paradigms concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Research Ethics & IRB
modules.titleZh: 研究伦理与伦理审查委员会
modules.objectives: Explain the historical events (Tuskegee, Milgram, Zimbardo) that led to modern research ethics frameworks; describe the core principles of the Belmont Report (respect for persons, beneficence, justice); explain the role of Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) in protecting human subjects.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §§3.1–3.2 — Human Research and Specific Ethical Issues
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Research Ethics & IRB; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Research Ethics & IRB evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Review this fictional proposal only: a researcher wants to recruit 14–17-year-old students through their teachers, record identifiable interviews about family conflict, and store files in a shared drive. Write an ethics review identifying consent/assent, coercion, confidentiality, data security, risk, benefit, justice, and withdrawal concerns. Redesign the proposal on paper; do not recruit or contact anyone. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: at least six concrete risks, Belmont-principle mapping, an age-appropriate consent/assent plan, secure-data plan, withdrawal procedure, and a revised proposal. Evaluation: 100% total — Research Ethics concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Developing Research Questions
modules.objectives: Distinguish between descriptive, explanatory, and evaluative research questions; explain what makes a research question researchable, specific, and significant; describe the relationship between research questions, hypotheses, and variables.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §§4.1–4.4 — Building an Empirical, Sociological Research Question
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Developing Research Questions; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Developing Research Questions evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Revise these supplied topics into researchable questions: “Is social media bad?”, “Why are students lazy?”, and “Does school matter?” For each, remove loaded language, define population and setting, identify whether the result is descriptive, explanatory, or evaluative, and operationalize the variables or indicators appropriate to each question. Use independent/dependent variable roles only for a question that investigates a relationship or effect; a descriptive question may instead define one outcome and its distribution. Select the strongest revised question and write a testable hypothesis. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: three before/after questions, scope and type labels, operational definitions appropriate to all three questions, one selected question, and one directional or nondirectional testable hypothesis. Evaluation: 100% total — Research Questions concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Literature Review
modules.objectives: Explain the purpose of a literature review in research; distinguish between primary and secondary sources; describe how to search academic databases, evaluate source credibility, and synthesize findings to identify research gaps.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §4.5 — Next Steps and Review of Existing Research
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Literature Review; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Literature Review evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Select a social science topic from a previous module. Using Google Scholar or your school library database, find three peer-reviewed journal articles on that topic. Write a 350-word mini-literature review that: (1) synthesizes the main findings across the three articles, (2) identifies what they agree on, (3) identifies a gap or debate that remains unresolved, and (4) explains how your own potential research could contribute to filling that gap. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: the final product, visible work or evidence, and a short explanation connecting each conclusion to Literature Review. Evaluation: 100% total — Literature Review concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); cross-source synthesis and a well-supported research-gap argument (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Quantitative Research Design
modules.objectives: Define quantitative research and explain its core logic; distinguish between cross-sectional, longitudinal, and panel designs; explain concepts of validity (internal and external), reliability, and generalizability in quantitative research.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §5.2 plus §§6.4 and 8.3 — Quantitative Design, Measurement Quality, and Survey Types Correction for this course: statistical significance does not measure relationship strength or practical importance and does not by itself establish causality; examine effect size and design separately.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Quantitative Research Design; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Quantitative Research Design evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Design a proposal, without recruiting participants, to study whether a four-week study-planning lesson affects assignment completion. Use this fictional setting: two existing Grade 10 classes of 25 students each; one class receives the lesson and one does not; baseline completion is available for both. Specify design type, independent/dependent variables, reliability check, threats to internal validity, external-validity limits, and the difference between a longitudinal design and a panel design. Do not claim that “measures what it claims” defines internal validity. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: a labeled design diagram, operational definitions, at least three alternative explanations, reliability plan, generalization limits, and precise cross-sectional/longitudinal/panel distinctions. Evaluation: 100% total — Quantitative Design concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Surveys & Questionnaires
modules.objectives: Explain the types of survey questions (open-ended, closed-ended, Likert scale, ranking); identify principles of good questionnaire design (clarity, neutrality, order effects); describe sampling strategies (random, stratified, convenience, snowball) and their implications for representativeness.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §§7.2–7.3 and 8.3–8.4 — Sampling and Questionnaire Design
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Surveys & Questionnaires; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Surveys & Questionnaires evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Build a 10-item questionnaire for the fictional question “How is after-school work associated with Grade 11 study time?” Use these supplied constraints: no names, ranges for weekly work hours, a seven-day recall period for study time, and one attention-check item. Include two Likert items, two categorical items, two numeric items, and four additional neutral items. Identify sampling frame, choose a probability sampling method, and diagnose two possible response biases. Do not administer the survey. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: ten numbered items meeting the type counts, neutral wording, one attention check, sampling frame and method, and two bias diagnoses with mitigation. Evaluation: 100% total — Survey Design concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Experimental & Quasi-Experimental Design
modules.objectives: Explain the logic of experimental research and why random assignment is important; distinguish between true experiments and quasi-experiments; define and identify threats to internal validity (confounding, selection bias, attrition); explain when experimental design is or is not feasible in social research.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Experimental & Quasi-Experimental Design; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Experimental & Quasi-Experimental Design evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Evaluate this fictional quasi-experiment: one school adopts a tutoring app and a nearby school does not; the app school began with lower scores, 15% of students leave before posttest, and teachers know which school received the app. Draw a design diagram, identify selection, attrition, expectation, and history threats, explain why random assignment balances observed and unobserved characteristics only in expectation, and propose two feasible design improvements. Do not run an experiment. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: the supplied case diagram, true-vs-quasi classification, four threat analyses, a careful random-assignment explanation, and two improvements. Evaluation: 100% total — Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Design concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Qualitative Research Design
modules.objectives: Explain the philosophy and goals of qualitative research; compare qualitative and quantitative approaches on key dimensions (generalizability, depth, objectivity); describe the main qualitative traditions (phenomenology, grounded theory, case study, narrative research, ethnography).
modules.readingNote: Saylor §5.2 — Choosing Qualitative or Quantitative Design Correction for this course: statistical significance does not measure relationship strength or practical importance and does not by itself establish causality; examine effect size and design separately.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Qualitative Research Design; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Supplied qualitative-traditions guide: phenomenology studies lived experience; grounded theory develops theory from iterative coding; case study investigates a bounded case with multiple evidence sources; narrative research analyzes stories across time; ethnography studies shared culture through sustained field engagement. Apply this guide only to the fictional proposal.
modules.assignment: Choose among phenomenology, grounded theory, case study, narrative research, and ethnography for each supplied goal: A lived experience of first-generation students; B process by which clubs recruit members; C one school’s response to a flood; D one refugee student’s education story; E culture and routines of a robotics team. Justify each match, then choose one and draft a proposal-only sampling and analysis plan. Do not assume qualitative methods are inherently superior. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: five method matches, five justifications tied to the goal, and one bounded proposal with sampling, data form, analysis steps, limits, and no participant contact. Evaluation: 100% total — Qualitative Design concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Interviews & Focus Groups
modules.objectives: Compare structured, semi-structured, and unstructured interview formats; explain how to develop an interview guide; describe the advantages and challenges of focus groups compared to individual interviews; identify ethical issues in interview research (confidentiality, rapport, power dynamics).
modules.readingNote: Saylor §§9.1–9.4 and §12.1 — Interview Techniques and Focus Groups
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Interviews & Focus Groups; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Interviews & Focus Groups evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: You want to understand the experiences of first-generation college students at your school. In 350 words, design a qualitative data collection plan: (1) choose between individual interviews and focus groups and justify your choice, (2) describe your interview format (structured, semi-structured, or unstructured) and explain why, (3) write three specific interview questions you would ask, (4) explain how you would ensure participants feel comfortable sharing sensitive experiences, and (5) describe how you would handle confidentiality of what participants share. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: the final product, visible work or evidence, and a short explanation connecting each conclusion to Interviews & Focus Groups. Evaluation: 100% total — Interviews & Focus Groups concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Observational Methods & Ethnography
modules.objectives: Distinguish between participant observation, non-participant observation, and ethnography; explain the continuum from covert to overt observation; describe how field notes are recorded and used; analyze the ethical challenges of ethnographic research.
modules.readingNote: Saylor §§10.1–10.4 — Field Research and Field Notes
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Observational Methods & Ethnography; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor worked reading — use the named section to complete the supplied Observational Methods & Ethnography evidence task; no outside participants or data collection are required.
modules.assignment: Code this fictional observation record: “At 3:02, four students enter the library. Two sit together and open laptops. At 3:07, one says, ‘Let’s split the questions.’ At 3:10, another student joins and asks for the worksheet. The observer feels the group appears comfortable, but cannot infer motivation.” Separate descriptive notes, direct quotation, and reflexive notes. Create four preliminary codes and one cautious analytic memo. No real observation or covert data collection is allowed. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: the complete supplied record, three note types, four codes linked to exact excerpts, a reflexive statement, one memo, and a clear boundary between observation and inference. Evaluation: 100% total — Observation and Ethnography concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Analyzing Quantitative Data
modules.objectives: Distinguish between descriptive and inferential statistics; calculate and interpret measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, standard deviation); explain the concept of statistical significance and p-values; identify appropriate visualizations for quantitative data.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e §2.7 — variance and sample/population standard deviation; for even n, median is the average of the two middle ordered values.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Analyzing Quantitative Data; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e §9.4 — interpret a p-value as a conditional probability under the null model, not the probability that the null is true. For the supplied n=20 assignment, use the average of positions 10 and 11 for the median and the n−1 denominator for sample SD.
modules.assignment: Analyze this complete fictional dataset of weekly study hours for 20 students: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 18. Order the values first; because n = 20, calculate the median as the average of positions 10 and 11. Calculate mean, median, mode, range, sample standard deviation using the n−1 denominator, and an outlier-resistant summary. Draw a labeled histogram or dot plot. Then interpret each statistic and explain why standard deviation is based on squared deviations rather than being the average absolute distance from the mean. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: all 20 values, visible calculation steps or spreadsheet formulas, sample-vs-population notation, labeled visualization, and interpretations including the 18-hour outlier. Evaluation: 100% total — Quantitative Data Analysis concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

modules.title: Analyzing Qualitative Data
modules.objectives: Explain the process of coding qualitative data (open coding, axial coding, selective coding); describe thematic analysis as a systematic approach to identifying patterns; explain how to establish trustworthiness in qualitative research (member checking, triangulation, thick description).
modules.readingNote: Saylor §10.5 — Analysis of Field Research Data
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Analyzing Qualitative Data; use with the exact Saylor section and the supplied fictional evidence.
modules.practiceNote: Saylor §10.5 plus supplied guide: open coding labels initial segments; axial/focused coding connects and consolidates categories; selective coding integrates categories around a central explanation. Member checking seeks participant feedback, triangulation compares sources/methods/researchers, and thick description supplies context. Apply these methods only to the four fictional excerpts.
modules.assignment: Analyze these fictional interview excerpts: A “Group chat reminders keep me on track, but constant alerts make me anxious”; B “I mute the chat during homework and check it later”; C “If nobody replies, I feel excluded”; D “Scheduled reminders help; random messages distract me.” Conduct open coding, group codes into at least two categories, propose two themes, create a codebook with definitions and inclusion/exclusion rules, and write a 250-word analytic memo with at least one negative or complicating case. Do not generalize beyond these four excerpts. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections and source links where used. Include: all four excerpts, line-linked open codes, codebook, categories, two themes, negative-case treatment, reflexivity note, and bounded conclusions. Evaluation: 100% total — Qualitative Data Analysis concept accuracy and correct reasoning (40%); complete evidence, data, calculations, or examples (30%); justified decisions tied to the supplied scenario (20%); clear organization and source attribution (10%).

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes social science research from everyday, informal knowledge?
options: Social science uses systematic, empirical methods with transparent procedures that can be evaluated and replicated
Social science uses large sample sizes while everyday knowledge uses small ones
Social science is conducted only by university professors
Everyday knowledge is always incorrect while social science is always right
quizQuestions.answer: Social science uses systematic, empirical methods with transparent procedures that can be evaluated and replicated
quizQuestions.explanation: Social science is 'scientific' because it applies systematic, empirical, transparent methods — data collection, analysis, reporting — that allow others to evaluate, criticize, and replicate findings.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of an 'empirical' research question in social science?
options: Should the minimum wage be raised to $20 per hour?
Does raising the minimum wage reduce teenage employment?
What is the right immigration policy?
Is capitalism fair?
quizQuestions.answer: Does raising the minimum wage reduce teenage employment?
quizQuestions.explanation: “Does raising the minimum wage reduce teenage employment?” is empirical because observable employment data can bear on it. The other choices ask what should happen or what is morally right, so they are normative.

quizQuestions.question: Which practice most directly makes a social-science claim open to independent evaluation?
options: Relying on intuition
Keeping procedures secret
Reporting methods, evidence, and limitations transparently
Using technical vocabulary
quizQuestions.answer: Reporting methods, evidence, and limitations transparently
quizQuestions.explanation: Transparent methods and evidence allow others to assess and replicate the work. This distinction follows the method’s definition and prevents a stronger inference than the design or evidence can support.

quizQuestions.question: Which social science discipline primarily studies individual behavior and mental processes? Name it and give one example research question from that discipline.
quizQuestions.answer: Psychology; for example, “How is sleep duration associated with working-memory performance among high school students?” Other accurate psychology questions earn full credit.
quizQuestions.explanation: Psychology studies behavior and mental processes. A complete answer identifies psychology and gives a specific empirical question rather than only a topic label.

quizQuestions.question: A 'positivist' research paradigm assumes that:
options: Social reality is subjective and constructed through human interpretation
Research should serve to empower oppressed groups
All social knowledge is relative to the researcher's cultural context
Social phenomena can be studied objectively using methods similar to natural science, producing generalizable laws
quizQuestions.answer: Social phenomena can be studied objectively using methods similar to natural science, producing generalizable laws
quizQuestions.explanation: Positivism holds that social reality exists independently of observers and can be measured objectively — emphasizing quantitative methods, hypothesis testing, and universal laws.

quizQuestions.question: 'Ontology' in research philosophy refers to:
options: Assumptions about the nature of reality — what exists and how it is structured
How a researcher collects and analyzes data
The theory of knowledge — what counts as valid evidence
The ethical principles guiding research practice
quizQuestions.answer: Assumptions about the nature of reality — what exists and how it is structured
quizQuestions.explanation: Ontology deals with assumptions about reality: does social reality exist independently of human minds (realism) or is it socially constructed (constructivism)?

quizQuestions.question: An interpretivist research approach would most likely use which method?
options: Randomized controlled experiment
In-depth interviews and thematic analysis of participants' subjective meanings
Large-scale national survey with statistical analysis
Analysis of economic indicators using regression models
quizQuestions.answer: In-depth interviews and thematic analysis of participants' subjective meanings
quizQuestions.explanation: Interpretivism seeks to understand the subjective meanings people give to social phenomena — privileging qualitative methods like interviews, ethnography, and discourse analysis.

quizQuestions.question: A critical research paradigm most directly asks how a social pattern is shaped by:
options: Planetary motion
Random error only
Power and inequality
Grammar rules
quizQuestions.answer: Power and inequality
quizQuestions.explanation: Critical approaches examine how structures, power, and inequality shape knowledge and social conditions.

quizQuestions.question: The Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972) is used as a foundational example in research ethics because:
options: It set the gold standard for informed consent procedures
It demonstrated that medical experiments can be conducted ethically on prisoners
It produced the first randomized controlled trial in medical history
Researchers deliberately withheld effective treatment from Black men with syphilis without their knowledge or consent, causing preventable suffering and death
quizQuestions.answer: Researchers deliberately withheld effective treatment from Black men with syphilis without their knowledge or consent, causing preventable suffering and death
quizQuestions.explanation: Tuskegee remains the defining case of research ethics violation: the US government knowingly denied Black men treatment for syphilis for 40 years to study disease progression — without consent, and despite penicillin becoming available as a cure.

quizQuestions.question: The Belmont Report's principle of 'respect for persons' primarily requires:
options: That researchers treat participants as autonomous individuals by obtaining informed consent
That research benefit society at large
That risks to participants be minimized relative to benefits
That research be distributed fairly across different social groups
quizQuestions.answer: That researchers treat participants as autonomous individuals by obtaining informed consent
quizQuestions.explanation: Respect for persons means recognizing individuals as autonomous agents capable of making their own decisions — operationalized through informed consent — and protecting those with diminished autonomy.

quizQuestions.question: Informed consent in human subjects research requires that participants:
options: Sign a legal contract agreeing to complete the study
Be fully informed of the study's nature, risks, and benefits, and voluntarily agree to participate without coercion
Receive payment for their participation
Have at least a high school education to understand the research
quizQuestions.answer: Be fully informed of the study's nature, risks, and benefits, and voluntarily agree to participate without coercion
quizQuestions.explanation: Informed consent requires disclosure of study purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, and the right to withdraw — and voluntary agreement free from coercion or undue incentive.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Research 'confidentiality' means that.
quizQuestions.answer: Protecting participant identities and data so private information is not disclosed to unauthorized people.
quizQuestions.explanation: Confidentiality means data can be collected but must be stored and reported in ways that protect participants.

quizQuestions.question: A 'descriptive' research question aims to:
options: Test a causal relationship between variables
Understand why a social phenomenon occurs by explaining its causes
Document and describe what a phenomenon looks like, how common it is, or how it is distributed
Evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention or program
quizQuestions.answer: Document and describe what a phenomenon looks like, how common it is, or how it is distributed
quizQuestions.explanation: Descriptive research asks 'what' — mapping the prevalence, characteristics, or distribution of a phenomenon — rather than 'why' (explanatory) or 'what works' (evaluative).

quizQuestions.question: A research hypothesis is best defined as:
options: A proven statement about the social world
The final conclusion of a research study
A general topic area chosen for investigation
A testable prediction about the relationship between variables, derived from theory or prior research
quizQuestions.answer: A testable prediction about the relationship between variables, derived from theory or prior research
quizQuestions.explanation: A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction — e.g., 'students who attend peer tutoring sessions will earn higher test scores than those who do not' — that can be evaluated with empirical evidence.

quizQuestions.question: In social science research, the 'independent variable' is:
options: The variable the researcher manipulates or measures as the presumed cause
The variable the researcher measures as an outcome
A variable that is statistically controlled in the analysis
The variable that describes the sample characteristics
quizQuestions.answer: The variable the researcher manipulates or measures as the presumed cause
quizQuestions.explanation: The independent variable (IV) is the presumed cause — it comes before (logically or temporally) the dependent variable (DV) and is what the researcher varies or measures to explain the outcome.

quizQuestions.question: Why is it problematic to have a research question like 'Is social media bad for teens?'
options: Social media cannot be studied scientifically
The question is normative and too broad — 'bad' is undefined, and the effects are likely complex and conditional rather than simply 'good' or 'bad'
Teen behavior is impossible to measure
Research on social media requires special government approval
quizQuestions.answer: The question is normative and too broad — 'bad' is undefined, and the effects are likely complex and conditional rather than simply 'good' or 'bad'
quizQuestions.explanation: Good research questions are empirical (not value judgments), specific (what aspect of social media? what outcome? for which teens?), and answerable with data — 'Is social media bad?' fails on all three grounds.

quizQuestions.question: The primary purpose of a literature review in a research project is to:
options: Prove that no one has studied the topic before
Demonstrate broad reading of non-academic sources
Synthesize existing knowledge on a topic, identify gaps, and position the new study within the field
Summarize the researcher's personal opinions on a topic
quizQuestions.answer: Synthesize existing knowledge on a topic, identify gaps, and position the new study within the field
quizQuestions.explanation: A literature review maps what is already known, identifies debates and gaps in existing research, and situates the new study's contribution within the scholarly conversation.

quizQuestions.question: A 'peer-reviewed' journal article is one that:
options: Has been read by at least 10 other students before publication
Is published by a university rather than a commercial publisher
Has received at least 100 citations from other scholars
Has been evaluated by independent experts in the field before publication to assess its scholarly merit
quizQuestions.answer: Has been evaluated by independent experts in the field before publication to assess its scholarly merit
quizQuestions.explanation: Peer review means that independent experts evaluate a manuscript's methodology, analysis, and contribution before publication — the primary quality control mechanism in academic publishing.

quizQuestions.question: Which action is synthesis rather than a source-by-source summary?
options: Grouping studies by competing explanations and comparing their evidence
Listing article titles alphabetically
Copying each abstract
Reporting only one study
quizQuestions.answer: Grouping studies by competing explanations and comparing their evidence
quizQuestions.explanation: Synthesis organizes sources around patterns, disagreements, and gaps. This distinction follows the method’s definition and prevents a stronger inference than the design or evidence can support.

quizQuestions.question: Which source is primary research?
options: A textbook chapter summarizing ten studies
A journal article reporting the authors’ original data and methods
A news article about a survey
An encyclopedia entry
quizQuestions.answer: A journal article reporting the authors’ original data and methods
quizQuestions.explanation: A primary research report presents the investigators’ original methods, data, and analysis.

quizQuestions.question: Quantitative research is best characterized by:
options: In-depth exploration of individual perspectives and meanings
Embedded fieldwork within a social group over an extended period
Numerical measurement of variables and statistical analysis to test hypotheses
Open-ended interviews and thematic coding
quizQuestions.answer: Numerical measurement of variables and statistical analysis to test hypotheses
quizQuestions.explanation: Quantitative research uses numerical data and statistical analysis to measure variables, test hypotheses, and generalize findings to broader populations.

quizQuestions.question: Internal validity concerns whether:
options: A measure has high face validity
The sample represents every country
The report is easy to read
The observed relationship can credibly be attributed to the proposed cause rather than confounds or alternative explanations
quizQuestions.answer: The observed relationship can credibly be attributed to the proposed cause rather than confounds or alternative explanations
quizQuestions.explanation: Internal validity is about credible causal interpretation; whether an instrument measures the intended construct is measurement or construct validity.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes longitudinal and panel designs?
options: Longitudinal is the broad category for repeated observations over time; a panel repeatedly observes the same units
Every longitudinal study follows the same individuals
Panel studies use only one time point
The terms always mean cross-sectional
quizQuestions.answer: Longitudinal is the broad category for repeated observations over time; a panel repeatedly observes the same units
quizQuestions.explanation: Panel studies are one type of longitudinal design; repeated cross-sectional trend studies also observe change over time but sample different units.

quizQuestions.question: Which design measures different samples from the same population at several time points?
options: Cross-sectional
Repeated cross-sectional trend study
Panel study
Case study
quizQuestions.answer: Repeated cross-sectional trend study
quizQuestions.explanation: A trend study samples the same population repeatedly; a panel follows the same individuals.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: 'external validity' in social research refers to.
quizQuestions.answer: The extent to which findings can generalize beyond the specific sample, setting, and study conditions.
quizQuestions.explanation: External validity asks whether results apply to other people, places, times, or situations.

quizQuestions.question: A Likert scale question asks respondents to:
options: Choose from a yes/no binary response
Select all answers that apply from a checklist
Rate their level of agreement or frequency on a continuum (e.g., Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree)
Write an open-ended response in their own words
quizQuestions.answer: Rate their level of agreement or frequency on a continuum (e.g., Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree)
quizQuestions.explanation: Likert scales capture intensity or degree of attitude across a range of options (e.g., 5-point: Strongly Agree, Agree, Neutral, Disagree, Strongly Disagree), providing ordinal data.

quizQuestions.question: A 'double-barreled' survey question is problematic because:
options: It asks the same question twice in different words
It is too long for respondents to understand
It uses academic jargon that respondents may not know
It combines two distinct issues in one question, making it impossible to know which part the respondent is answering
quizQuestions.answer: It combines two distinct issues in one question, making it impossible to know which part the respondent is answering
quizQuestions.explanation: Double-barreled questions (e.g., 'Do you support higher taxes and more government spending?') combine two issues — respondents may agree with one but not the other, making answers uninterpretable.

quizQuestions.question: Which item is double-barreled?
options: How satisfied are you with teacher feedback and course pacing?
How many days did you study last week?
What grade are you in?
Did you attend tutoring this month?
quizQuestions.answer: How satisfied are you with teacher feedback and course pacing?
quizQuestions.explanation: It asks about two issues in one response. This distinction follows the method’s definition and prevents a stronger inference than the design or evidence can support.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Survey 'response bias' occurs when.
quizQuestions.answer: Participants answer inaccurately or systematically distort responses because of wording, social desirability, memory, or survey context.
quizQuestions.explanation: Response bias affects the accuracy of survey data even when the sample was selected well.

quizQuestions.question: The key feature that distinguishes a 'true experiment' from other research designs is:
options: The use of a large sample size
Random assignment of participants to treatment and control conditions
The collection of both quantitative and qualitative data
The use of multiple dependent variables
quizQuestions.answer: Random assignment of participants to treatment and control conditions
quizQuestions.explanation: Random assignment makes systematic pre-treatment differences less likely and balances observed and unobserved characteristics in expectation. A particular realized sample can still be imbalanced by chance.

quizQuestions.question: A 'control group' in an experiment serves the purpose of:
options: Receiving the treatment to see if it works
Ensuring all participants behave ethically during the study
Providing a comparison baseline so the effect of the treatment can be isolated
Testing multiple treatments simultaneously
quizQuestions.answer: Providing a comparison baseline so the effect of the treatment can be isolated
quizQuestions.explanation: The control group receives no treatment (or a placebo), allowing researchers to compare outcomes with the treatment group and attribute differences to the experimental manipulation.

quizQuestions.question: A quasi-experimental design differs from a true experiment in that:
options: It does not collect outcome data
It is only used in laboratory settings
It relies entirely on qualitative data
It lacks random assignment to conditions, making causal claims more tenuous
quizQuestions.answer: It lacks random assignment to conditions, making causal claims more tenuous
quizQuestions.explanation: Quasi-experiments compare pre-existing groups or use natural variation (e.g., comparing schools that adopted a program vs. those that didn't) — without random assignment, so unmeasured confounders remain a threat.

quizQuestions.question: Why can random assignment support causal inference?
options: It balances observed and unobserved characteristics in expectation, reducing systematic selection differences
It guarantees identical groups
It increases the sample size automatically
It removes all attrition
quizQuestions.answer: It balances observed and unobserved characteristics in expectation, reducing systematic selection differences
quizQuestions.explanation: Randomization reduces systematic pre-treatment differences but does not guarantee exact balance or remove every later threat.

quizQuestions.question: Qualitative research is most appropriate when the research goal is to:
options: Test a specific hypothesis with a large representative sample
Deeply understand the meanings, experiences, and perspectives of participants in their natural context
Measure the prevalence of a behavior across a national population
Establish a mathematical relationship between two variables
quizQuestions.answer: Deeply understand the meanings, experiences, and perspectives of participants in their natural context
quizQuestions.explanation: Qualitative research excels at exploring 'how' and 'why' questions — generating rich, contextual understanding of human experience, meaning-making, and social processes.

quizQuestions.question: Grounded theory as a qualitative tradition aims to:
options: Test an existing theory against new empirical data
Describe the lived experience of a specific group
Develop new theoretical explanations directly from systematic analysis of collected data
Produce thick descriptions of cultural practices in their natural setting
quizQuestions.answer: Develop new theoretical explanations directly from systematic analysis of collected data
quizQuestions.explanation: Grounded theory (Glaser & Strauss) builds theory inductively from data through constant comparative analysis — the theory 'emerges from' or is 'grounded in' the data rather than imposed from outside.

quizQuestions.question: Phenomenology as a qualitative research tradition focuses on:
options: Understanding how social structures shape group behavior
Observing and documenting cultural practices over extended periods
Developing new social theories from interview data
Describing the lived experience of a phenomenon from the perspective of those who experienced it
quizQuestions.answer: Describing the lived experience of a phenomenon from the perspective of those who experienced it
quizQuestions.explanation: Phenomenology explores the subjective, first-person experience of a phenomenon — asking 'What is it like to experience X?' — seeking the essential structure of that experience as described by participants.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: A case study research design in social science involves.
quizQuestions.answer: An in-depth investigation of one person, group, event, organization, or setting using multiple sources of evidence.
quizQuestions.explanation: Case studies trade broad generalization for deep contextual understanding.

quizQuestions.question: A 'semi-structured interview' is characterized by:
options: A prepared guide with key topics and questions but flexibility to probe and follow unexpected threads
A fixed set of identical questions asked in the same order to all participants
An open-ended conversation with no predetermined questions
Standardized questions read from a computer with no interviewer interaction
quizQuestions.answer: A prepared guide with key topics and questions but flexibility to probe and follow unexpected threads
quizQuestions.explanation: Semi-structured interviews provide structure (ensuring key topics are covered) while allowing flexibility — the interviewer can ask follow-up probes, explore unexpected themes, and adapt to each participant's responses.

quizQuestions.question: Focus groups differ from individual interviews primarily in that:
options: Focus groups produce more statistically reliable data
Focus group dynamics allow participant interaction, which can generate collective meanings and social perspectives not available in individual interviews
Focus groups are more ethical because participants can monitor each other
Focus groups are always conducted online
quizQuestions.answer: Focus group dynamics allow participant interaction, which can generate collective meanings and social perspectives not available in individual interviews
quizQuestions.explanation: Focus groups harness group interaction — participants discuss, debate, and build on each other's views — revealing shared social meanings and group norms that individual interviews cannot capture.

quizQuestions.question: 'Rapport' in qualitative interviewing refers to:
options: The researcher's academic credentials that establish credibility
The formal consent procedure completed before the interview
A trusting relationship between interviewer and participant that encourages open, honest sharing
The audio recording used to accurately transcribe the interview
quizQuestions.answer: A trusting relationship between interviewer and participant that encourages open, honest sharing
quizQuestions.explanation: Rapport is the warm, trusting relationship between interviewer and participant — essential for getting honest, in-depth responses, especially on sensitive topics.

quizQuestions.question: In interview research, 'probing' questions are used to:
options: Introduce new topics not previously discussed
Challenge the participant's credibility or test their knowledge
Conclude the interview and signal the conversation is ending
Follow up an initial response to get more depth, detail, or clarification
quizQuestions.answer: Follow up an initial response to get more depth, detail, or clarification
quizQuestions.explanation: Probes (e.g., 'Can you tell me more about that?' or 'What do you mean by X?') encourage participants to elaborate, provide examples, or clarify ambiguous statements.

quizQuestions.question: In 'participant observation,' the researcher:
options: Fully embeds within the social group being studied, participating in activities while also observing
Observes participants through a one-way mirror without their knowledge
Analyzes videos of social interactions without being present
Surveys participants about their observations of others
quizQuestions.answer: Fully embeds within the social group being studied, participating in activities while also observing
quizQuestions.explanation: Participant observation involves the researcher joining the group or setting being studied — participating in activities to gain insider understanding while also systematically observing.

quizQuestions.question: 'Going native' in ethnographic research refers to the risk that:
options: The researcher adopts the local language of the community studied
The researcher becomes so immersed in the group that they lose their analytical perspective and objectivity
Participants refuse to interact with an outsider researcher
The researcher's presence changes participants' behavior
quizQuestions.answer: The researcher becomes so immersed in the group that they lose their analytical perspective and objectivity
quizQuestions.explanation: Going native is a key danger in participant observation: the researcher becomes so integrated into the community that they can no longer maintain critical analytical distance, seeing the group only from within.

quizQuestions.question: Which field-note statement is primarily descriptive?
options: The group was definitely unmotivated
The researcher’s identity caused every response
Three participants entered at 2:05 and sat at separate tables
This proves the theory
quizQuestions.answer: Three participants entered at 2:05 and sat at separate tables
quizQuestions.explanation: Descriptive notes record observable actions before interpretation. This distinction follows the method’s definition and prevents a stronger inference than the design or evidence can support.

quizQuestions.question: An overt observer should protect privacy by:
options: Publishing names for transparency
Secretly expanding the study
Posting raw notes publicly
Recording only data justified by consent and the approved plan, then securing identifiers
quizQuestions.answer: Recording only data justified by consent and the approved plan, then securing identifiers
quizQuestions.explanation: Ethical fieldwork limits collection, respects consent, and protects identifiable data. This distinction follows the method’s definition and prevents a stronger inference than the design or evidence can support.

quizQuestions.question: The mean, median, and mode are all measures of:
options: Central tendency — the typical or representative value in a dataset
The spread or variability of a dataset
Statistical significance between two groups
The reliability of a measurement instrument
quizQuestions.answer: Central tendency — the typical or representative value in a dataset
quizQuestions.explanation: Mean, median, and mode are the three measures of central tendency — each describing a different sense of what is 'typical' or 'central' in a distribution of values.

quizQuestions.question: For a strongly right-skewed distribution with extreme high outliers, which measure of center is usually most resistant to distortion?
options: Mean
Median
Range
Standard deviation
quizQuestions.answer: Median
quizQuestions.explanation: The median depends on order rather than the magnitude of extremes, making it resistant to outliers.

quizQuestions.question: Standard deviation describes:
options: The arithmetic average of absolute distances from the mean
The difference between maximum and minimum only
Typical spread around the mean based on squared deviations, expressed in the original units
The middle observation
quizQuestions.answer: Typical spread around the mean based on squared deviations, expressed in the original units
quizQuestions.explanation: Variance averages squared deviations (with the appropriate denominator); standard deviation is its square root. It is not mean absolute deviation.

quizQuestions.question: Which graph best displays the distribution of one quantitative variable such as weekly study hours?
options: Histogram
Pie chart of interview themes
Organizational chart
Flowchart
quizQuestions.answer: Histogram
quizQuestions.explanation: A histogram groups quantitative values into intervals and shows their frequency distribution, making shape, spread, and possible outliers visible.

quizQuestions.question: A study reports p = .03 for a test conducted under a stated null hypothesis. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 3% probability the null hypothesis is true
If the null model and assumptions hold, results this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time
The effect has a 97% chance of replicating
The effect is necessarily large
quizQuestions.answer: If the null model and assumptions hold, results this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time
quizQuestions.explanation: A p-value is conditional on the null model and assumptions. It is not the probability that the null is true, a replication probability, or a measure of effect size.

quizQuestions.question: In qualitative data analysis, 'coding' refers to:
options: Systematically labeling segments of text with tags (codes) that represent their meaning or content
Converting interview responses into numerical scores
Encrypting participant data to protect confidentiality
Writing computer programs to process survey data
quizQuestions.answer: Systematically labeling segments of text with tags (codes) that represent their meaning or content
quizQuestions.explanation: Coding is the process of attaching labels (codes) to segments of qualitative data (interview transcripts, field notes) that capture the key idea, theme, or concept represented in that passage.

quizQuestions.question: Thematic analysis in qualitative research involves:
options: Counting how many times key words appear in a text
Identifying and interpreting recurring patterns of meaning (themes) across a dataset
Analyzing the grammatical structure of participants' language
Comparing statistical distributions across different participant groups
quizQuestions.answer: Identifying and interpreting recurring patterns of meaning (themes) across a dataset
quizQuestions.explanation: Thematic analysis systematically identifies, analyzes, and reports patterns (themes) within qualitative data — moving from initial codes to broader themes that capture shared meaning.

quizQuestions.question: What should a qualitative codebook include?
options: Only theme names
Participant contact details
Code names, definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules, and examples
A p-value for every quote
quizQuestions.answer: Code names, definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules, and examples
quizQuestions.explanation: A codebook supports consistent, transparent application of codes. This distinction follows the method’s definition and prevents a stronger inference than the design or evidence can support.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Researcher 'reflexivity' in qualitative research requires the researcher to.
quizQuestions.answer: Examine how the researcher's identity, assumptions, role, and choices may influence data collection and interpretation.
quizQuestions.explanation: Reflexivity is especially important in qualitative research because the researcher is part of the interpretive process.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'social science research' as distinct from everyday knowledge?
options: Social science is always conducted in a laboratory
Social science always produces definitive, final answers
Social science only studies individual behavior, not groups
Social science uses systematic, empirical, and transparent methods that can be independently evaluated and replicated
questions.answer: Social science uses systematic, empirical, and transparent methods that can be independently evaluated and replicated
questions.explanation: Social science research is distinguished by its systematic methodology: defined procedures, empirical evidence, transparent reporting, and openness to criticism and replication.

questions.question: A positivist research paradigm assumes that social phenomena:
options: Can be studied objectively through empirical methods, producing generalizable laws
Can only be understood from the insider perspective of participants
Should be studied primarily to promote social justice and equity
Are entirely shaped by language and cultural interpretation
questions.answer: Can be studied objectively through empirical methods, producing generalizable laws
questions.explanation: Positivism holds that an objective social reality exists and can be measured using scientific methods — privileging quantitative data, hypothesis testing, and statistical generalization.

questions.question: The Tuskegee Syphilis Study violated which core principle of the Belmont Report?
options: Beneficence only
Respect for persons (informed consent) and beneficence (withholding effective treatment) and justice (targeting a vulnerable racial group)
Justice only
None — the study followed all ethical standards of its time
questions.answer: Respect for persons (informed consent) and beneficence (withholding effective treatment) and justice (targeting a vulnerable racial group)
questions.explanation: Tuskegee violated all three Belmont principles: men were not informed they had syphilis (respect for persons), they were denied treatment (non-maleficence/beneficence), and the study exploited Black men in Alabama (justice).

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement? A research hypothesis must be:
options: A personal opinion that cannot be measured
A final conclusion written before data collection
A specific, testable prediction about the relationship between variables
A list of sources used in the study
questions.answer: A specific, testable prediction about the relationship between variables
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: A specific, testable prediction about the relationship between variables.

questions.question: The purpose of a literature review in social science research is primarily to:
options: Show that the researcher has read as many books as possible
Establish that no prior research exists on the topic
Summarize the researcher's personal experience with the topic
Synthesize existing knowledge, identify gaps, and position the new study within the scholarly conversation
questions.answer: Synthesize existing knowledge, identify gaps, and position the new study within the scholarly conversation
questions.explanation: A literature review maps what is known about a topic, identifies debates and gaps, and explains how the new study contributes to — or departs from — the existing body of knowledge.

questions.question: Internal validity is strongest when:
options: Alternative explanations for the observed effect have been credibly ruled out
The measure looks plausible
The sample is large but confounded
The report uses technical terms
questions.answer: Alternative explanations for the observed effect have been credibly ruled out
questions.explanation: Internal validity concerns causal credibility and control of confounds, not whether a measure captures a construct.

questions.question: When is stratified random sampling preferable to simple random sampling?
options: Never; simple random sampling is universally best
When important subgroups must be represented and a usable sampling frame identifies those strata
Only when no population list exists
Whenever researchers want volunteers
questions.answer: When important subgroups must be represented and a usable sampling frame identifies those strata
questions.explanation: The best probability design depends on the research goal, population structure, frame, cost, and desired subgroup precision.

questions.question: Random assignment in an experiment serves which key purpose?
options: Ensuring all participants complete the study without dropping out
Guaranteeing that the hypothesis will be supported
Making treatment and control groups comparable before the treatment
Replacing the need for ethical review
questions.answer: Making treatment and control groups comparable before the treatment
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Making treatment and control groups comparable before the treatment.

questions.question: For an in-depth study of meaning and lived experience, qualitative research is most appropriate when the goal is to:
options: Test a specific hypothesis with measurable variables
Estimate the percentage of people who hold a particular opinion
Establish a causal relationship between two variables
Understand the subjective meanings and experiences of participants in depth
questions.answer: Understand the subjective meanings and experiences of participants in depth
questions.explanation: Qualitative research excels at exploratory, in-depth understanding of complex social phenomena, meanings, and processes — where statistical measurement and generalization are less important than contextual richness.

questions.question: A researcher wants proportional representation from each grade level before randomly selecting students within grades. Which sampling method fits?
options: Convenience sampling
Snowball sampling
Stratified random sampling
Purposive sampling
questions.answer: Stratified random sampling
questions.explanation: Stratified random sampling divides the population into relevant strata, then randomly samples within each, supporting planned subgroup representation.

questions.question: Which change most directly improves the reliability of a multi-item survey scale?
options: Use consistent items that measure the same construct and test their agreement
Replace all items with one vague question
Recruit only volunteers who agree with the researcher
Remove the response scale
questions.answer: Use consistent items that measure the same construct and test their agreement
questions.explanation: Reliability concerns consistency of measurement; related items and an appropriate consistency check provide evidence that the scale yields stable, coherent scores.

questions.question: Which statement best describes synthesis in a literature review?
options: List each source separately without comparison
Compare patterns, disagreements, methods, and gaps across sources
Quote only the newest article
Count citations without reading methods
questions.answer: Compare patterns, disagreements, methods, and gaps across sources
questions.explanation: Synthesis organizes evidence across studies to show convergence, differences, limitations, and unanswered questions rather than producing isolated summaries.

questions.question: The 'dependent variable' in a research study is:
options: The variable the researcher controls or manipulates
A control variable held constant throughout the study
The demographic characteristics of study participants
The outcome the researcher measures — what is presumed to be caused or influenced by the independent variable
questions.answer: The outcome the researcher measures — what is presumed to be caused or influenced by the independent variable
questions.explanation: The dependent variable (DV) is the outcome being studied — it 'depends on' the independent variable and is measured to see if the presumed cause had an effect.

questions.question: A 'double-barreled' survey question is problematic because it:
questions.answer: Asks about two issues at once, making it impossible to know which part the respondent is answering.
questions.explanation: Double-barreled questions create ambiguous data because agreement with one part may not mean agreement with the other.

questions.question: Inductive reasoning in social science research moves from:
options: Specific observations toward broader patterns and theoretical explanations
General theory to specific hypothesis to data collection
Statistical models to mathematical predictions about behavior
Policy recommendations to research questions to data
questions.answer: Specific observations toward broader patterns and theoretical explanations
questions.explanation: Inductive research begins with data and observations, then builds upward toward patterns and theoretical explanations — contrasted with deductive research that starts with theory and tests specific hypotheses.

questions.question: In this course, which philosophical paradigm holds that social reality is socially constructed through human interaction and interpretation?
options: Positivism
Interpretivism
Determinism
Utilitarianism
questions.answer: Interpretivism
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Interpretivism. This reinforces the Research Methods in Social Science final concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: The Belmont Report's principle of 'justice' requires that:
options: Research benefits should outweigh risks to participants
Researchers should be legally prosecuted for ethical violations
Research burdens and benefits should be distributed fairly, not imposed on vulnerable groups for the benefit of others
All participants should receive identical treatment during the study
questions.answer: Research burdens and benefits should be distributed fairly, not imposed on vulnerable groups for the benefit of others
questions.explanation: Justice requires that neither the burdens of research nor the benefits be unfairly concentrated — historically vulnerable groups (prisoners, poor patients, minorities) should not bear risks for studies that primarily benefit others.

questions.question: Operationalization in social science research refers to:
options: The process of gaining ethical approval from an IRB
Writing the methods section of a research report
Selecting the most appropriate statistical test for the data
Defining precisely how abstract concepts will be measured in a specific study
questions.answer: Defining precisely how abstract concepts will be measured in a specific study
questions.explanation: Operationalization converts abstract constructs (intelligence, wellbeing, political engagement) into concrete, measurable indicators — a crucial step that links theory to empirical data.

questions.question: External validity in research is most directly threatened by:
options: Using a convenience sample that differs systematically from the target population
Confounding variables that influence the outcome
Random measurement error in questionnaire responses
The placebo effect in experimental conditions
questions.answer: Using a convenience sample that differs systematically from the target population
questions.explanation: External validity — generalizability — is threatened when the sample is not representative of the intended population, meaning findings may not apply beyond the specific sample studied.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement? Snowball sampling is most useful for studying:
options: Only nationally representative survey panels
Hard-to-reach or hidden populations
Laboratory animals in controlled experiments
Randomly generated computer data
questions.answer: Hard-to-reach or hidden populations
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Hard-to-reach or hidden populations. This reinforces the Research Methods in Social Science final concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: A quasi-experimental study lacks which key element of a true experiment, and why does that difference weaken causal inference?
questions.answer: It lacks random assignment to treatment and control conditions; without random assignment, pre-existing group differences can remain plausible alternative explanations.
questions.explanation: A complete answer identifies random assignment and connects its absence to selection differences or confounding rather than merely naming the design.

questions.question: Grounded theory as a qualitative approach is distinctive because it:
options: Tests a theory developed before data collection begins
Relies exclusively on secondary data sources
Builds new theoretical explanations inductively from systematic analysis of collected data
Is only used for studying small organizations
questions.answer: Builds new theoretical explanations inductively from systematic analysis of collected data
questions.explanation: Grounded theory builds theory from data through constant comparative analysis — the researcher lets theory 'emerge from' the data rather than imposing a pre-existing framework.

questions.question: The Hawthorne effect (observer effect) poses a threat to observational research because:
options: Researchers misinterpret behavior due to their own cultural biases
Field observation is more time-consuming than surveys
Observers cannot be in two places simultaneously
Participants change their behavior when they know they are being observed, making behavior less natural
questions.answer: Participants change their behavior when they know they are being observed, making behavior less natural
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne effect — documented in factory productivity studies — shows that awareness of being studied changes behavior, potentially invalidating naturalistic observations.

questions.question: What does standard deviation measure?
options: Spread around the mean using the square root of variance
The middle-ranked score
The most common score
The distance between maximum and minimum only
questions.answer: Spread around the mean using the square root of variance
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and is expressed in the variable’s original units.

questions.question: In qualitative research, 'triangulation' improves trustworthiness by:
options: Cross-checking findings using multiple data sources, methods, or researchers to identify convergence
Deleting excerpts that do not fit the first theme
Using only one interview and one coder
Reporting a theme without linking it to evidence
questions.answer: Cross-checking findings using multiple data sources, methods, or researchers to identify convergence
questions.explanation: Triangulation compares evidence across sources, methods, or researchers to examine convergence and divergence. It does not mean discarding contrary evidence or relying on an unsupported single source.

questions.question: A result reported as p = .03 means:
options: There is a 3% probability the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% probability the effect will replicate
Assuming the null hypothesis and analysis model are correct, results this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time
The effect is necessarily important
questions.answer: Assuming the null hypothesis and analysis model are correct, results this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time
questions.explanation: A p-value is conditional on the null hypothesis and model; it is not the probability that the null is true or a measure of practical importance.

questions.question: 'Member checking' as a qualitative trustworthiness strategy involves:
options: Verifying all participants are eligible members of the study population
Having all research team members independently code the data and compare results
Cross-referencing interview data with publicly available documentary evidence
Sharing preliminary findings with participants to check whether the analysis accurately reflects their experiences
questions.answer: Sharing preliminary findings with participants to check whether the analysis accurately reflects their experiences
questions.explanation: Member checking returns interpretations to participants for verification — allowing them to confirm, correct, or expand on the researcher's analysis, improving accuracy and respondent validation.

questions.question: Which revision turns “Is social media bad for teens?” into a more researchable descriptive question?
options: Is social media evil?
How many minutes per day do Grade 10 students at School X report using social media during a seven-day period?
Should all teenagers stop using phones?
Why are teens irresponsible online?
questions.answer: How many minutes per day do Grade 10 students at School X report using social media during a seven-day period?
questions.explanation: The revised question defines a population, setting, measure, and recall period without loaded language or an unsupported causal claim.

questions.question: Researcher 'reflexivity' in qualitative research requires the researcher to:
options: Actively reflect on and disclose how their identity, assumptions, and positionality may influence data collection and interpretation
Remain completely objective by suppressing personal knowledge
Only study phenomena they have no personal connection to
Use structured instruments to eliminate subjective judgment
questions.answer: Actively reflect on and disclose how their identity, assumptions, and positionality may influence data collection and interpretation
questions.explanation: Reflexivity acknowledges that researchers bring their own social position, values, and assumptions into the research — and requires ongoing critical examination of how these shape what is seen, asked, and interpreted.

questions.question: Reporting research limitations is important in a scientific report primarily because:
options: It shows the researcher had inadequate funding
It demonstrates scholarly integrity, contextualizes findings to prevent over-generalization, and guides future researchers
It is only required for studies that found non-significant results
It is required by law in most countries for published research
questions.answer: It demonstrates scholarly integrity, contextualizes findings to prevent over-generalization, and guides future researchers
questions.explanation: Reporting limitations honestly is a mark of good science — it helps readers correctly interpret findings, avoids misleading applications, and identifies specific directions for future research improvements.

questions.question: Which survey item is neutral and asks only one issue?
options: How satisfied are you with helpful teachers and fair grading?
How many days in the past seven did you study for at least 30 minutes?
Don’t you agree the new schedule is better?
Why do students waste time after school?
questions.answer: How many days in the past seven did you study for at least 30 minutes?
questions.explanation: It uses a defined recall period, asks one behavior, and avoids leading or judgmental language.

questions.question: Which strategy most directly strengthens trustworthiness by checking whether a qualitative interpretation fits participants’ intended meanings?
options: Member checking
Convenience sampling
Increasing the p-value
Removing negative cases
questions.answer: Member checking
questions.explanation: Member checking invites participants to comment on whether an interpretation reflects their intended meanings; it does not replace reflexivity or other evidence checks.

questions.question: Social desirability bias in survey research occurs when:
options: Respondents answer in the way they believe is socially acceptable rather than reflecting their true attitudes or behaviors
Respondents randomly skip questions they find difficult
Researchers design surveys around topics they personally prefer
Survey questions are arranged in a socially logical order
questions.answer: Respondents answer in the way they believe is socially acceptable rather than reflecting their true attitudes or behaviors
questions.explanation: Social desirability bias leads respondents to underreport stigmatized behaviors (drug use, prejudice) and overreport virtuous ones (voting, charitable giving) — distorting data on sensitive topics.

questions.question: Which study is specifically a panel design?
options: A one-time survey of seniors
Annual surveys that recontact the same 500 people
Annual surveys of different national samples
Interviews with five people on one day
questions.answer: Annual surveys that recontact the same 500 people
questions.explanation: A panel repeatedly observes the same units over time; it is one type of longitudinal design.

questions.question: Before collecting identifiable interview data in a human-participant study for which consent is required, what approvals and participant protection are needed?
questions.answer: Appropriate institutional ethics review or approval and informed consent (plus assent/parental permission where applicable) are required before collection. Any consent waiver must be authorized by the responsible review body, not declared by the student researcher.
questions.explanation: Researchers must obtain required oversight and protect voluntary participation, risk disclosure, confidentiality, and withdrawal rights. Authorized exceptions are determined through institutional review.
